title: Baden development charge complaint and 2025 budget adjustments
subtitle: Also: encampment security funding, U.S. tariff response, accessibility report, and key cultural institution funding allocations.
overview: The Administration and Finance Committee dismissed a development charges complaint about a 23-unit brownfield housing project at 162 Snyder's Road East in Baden {{vote:m1}}. The complainant wanted a full credit for cleanup costs. Staff said the ministry's acknowledgment came after the 2021 deadline, so only the 50% credit applies. The committee's decision on a complaint is final, though it can be appealed. A councillor asked staff to revise the by-law wording to avoid similar disputes.

On the 2025 budget, the committee recommended final adjustments to several operating lines that affect the tax levy {{vote:m2}}. It removed a proposed cut to encampment security {{vote:m3}}, and staff must return with a replacement for that $349,766. Council will consider these recommendations later.

The committee also recommended a response to possible U.S. tariffs, including a procurement review and an action plan for local businesses, including agriculture {{vote:m4}}. It received reports on accessibility and on 2025 key cultural institution funding for information. Staff were directed to look at an upper funding limit for those institutions.

decisions.detail: The committee dismissed the complaint about 162 Snyder's Road East {{vote:m1}}, so the 50% brownfield credit stays in place rather than the full credit.
The committee recommended amending 2025 operating budget lines, including supplies, equipment, professional fees and travel, that affect the tax levy {{vote:m2}}.
The committee recommended striking the proposed encampment security reduction from the budget adjustments {{vote:m3}}, with staff to propose a replacement for $349,766.

The committee recommended that staff explore limiting tariff impacts on regional services, review procurement for made-in-Canada provisions, and ask the Waterloo Economic Development Corporation (WEDC) to develop an action plan for local businesses, including agriculture {{vote:m4}}.

debate: On the Baden complaint, staff argued that "issued" means the ministry's acknowledgment letter and registry entry in January 2022, after the deadline. They said the certification date is unreliable because the ministry can reject a submission, as it did in this case. Staff also warned of a precedent affecting perhaps five to ten other properties.

The complainant's lawyer argued that the Environmental Protection Act speaks of certifying and filing records of site condition, not issuing them. On that reading, "issued" in the by-law should mean the October 2021 certification date. The lawyer said the site had been cleaned up, the project delivered rental housing, and the ministry's review time pushed it past the deadline.

Councillors split. Some were sympathetic and pointed to provincial review delays and the intent of the brownfield program. Others said deadlines must hold, that development charge credits fall on taxpayers, and that the developer knew in December that the decision might come after January 1.

On the budget, one councillor said the water and wastewater cuts could put drinking water at risk and should not have been touched. Staff said those items did not affect the levy and were not being adopted. Councillors also questioned the road salt and bus parts reductions, the cancelled 211 contract and the lack of travel and conference savings. Staff said road maintenance would not be reduced, though a harsh winter is a budget risk.

On the tariff motion, councillors raised effects on smaller exporters and vulnerable residents, and on the cost of procurement that depends on U.S.-built equipment. Agriculture was added to the action plan wording.
